tagline: Across former borderlands, a royal-road corridor leads toward the Mississippi.
intro: Louisiana Colonial Trails is a state scenic byway spread across several highways. Its LA 6 and US 84 sections connect the Texas line with the Mississippi at Natchez through Clarence. Along the way, Grand Ecore stands on a Red River bluff, while Vidalia faces Natchez across the Mississippi. Other branches reach Jena and Marksville, with a loop through Sicily Island. At Grand Ecore, the bluff rises eighty feet above the Red River; in Natchitoches, Front Street’s brick paving overlooks the river walk.

LA 6 roughly follows El Camino Real de los Tejas, an older Spanish colonial route whose Louisiana leg ended at Natchitoches. Its Sabine River ferry operated from around 1795 until the Gaines-Pendleton Bridge replaced it in 1937. The historic trail and the modern scenic-byway network have different extents: the byway’s US 84 section continues east from Clarence to the Mississippi state line.

For a west-to-east journey, follow LA 6 from the Texas line toward Clarence. Fort Jesup lies northeast of Many; Los Adaes is a separate stop near Robeline on LA 485. After Natchitoches, LA 6 reaches Grand Ecore on the Red River. At Clarence, US 84 carries the journey toward Vidalia and the bridge to Natchez.

moments.title: Fort Jesup
moments.text: The kitchen of Enlisted Barracks 4 was Fort Jesup’s only surviving building by the 1930s. Residents of Many raised money to restore it and turn the grounds into a park. Zachary Taylor established the post in 1822 near the former Neutral Strip. That disputed territory lay between the Sabine River and Arroyo Hondo; Spain and the United States had agreed to keep their armed forces out. The army operated the post until 1846; Louisiana’s Office of State Parks acquired the site in 1956. The kitchen was restored, while an officers’ quarters building was reconstructed to serve as a museum.

moments.title: Los Adaes
moments.text: Los Adaes combined a Franciscan mission with a presidio, a Spanish military post, near present-day Robeline. Spain established the outpost to counter French influence in Louisiana. Yet distance from other Spanish settlements led its residents to trade with the French at neighboring Natchitoches. The name comes from the Indigenous Adai people, whom the missionaries sought to convert. In 1773, Spanish authorities forced the settlers to move to San Antonio. Many died on the journey or soon after arriving. The site is preserved as Los Adaes State Historic Site. Its archaeological record includes both Spanish colonial and Adai culture.

moments.title: Natchitoches
moments.text: Front Street’s bricks were lifted, numbered and cleaned during a restoration that repaired utilities, drainage and the foundation underneath. The brick street overlooks the downtown river walk. Natchitoches began in 1714 as a French trading outpost on the Red River, near a village of the Natchitoches people. In the 1820s and early 1830s, cotton arrived overland from east Texas for transfer to boats bound down the Red River to New Orleans. When the Red River changed course, it bypassed the town and severed its commercial connection to the Mississippi. Cane River Lake occupies the former river course.
